It was a low building, whitewashed, cold as a spring house inside even in August, and it smelled of milk and steam and hot iron, and you could hear the engine going before you came round the last turn. Ansel Keddie ran it. He went up there in ninety-five, the year before they opened it, to get it ready, and he tested that first summer too, and he was still there when I was a girl big enough to ride on the wagon with my father, so you can count that up and see how long a man can stand in one room.

He wrote in it standing up at a slope desk by the window where the light came in. If a man came in and asked him what his milk had done, he did not have to hunt. He turned to the day and he read it off. He tested a thousand cans a week and never a blot in that book, and I heard my father say more than once that if the rest of the world kept its accounts the way Ansel Keddie kept his there would be no lawyers in Ashlin. The curd comes soft and it will not knit; you get a slack, weak body and your yield is down, and you can stand at the vat and see your money going out with the whey. ### Story 1 — The Rule That Made a Figure into Money

**Who.** The farmers of the Larrow Valley, Ordell County; Gideon Vose, their first president; Effie Loomis, secretary 1901–1940, who kept and later mourned the record.

**What happened, and when.** In 1889 the farmers met at Larrow Green — in the schoolhouse, in cold weather, very late, with somebody's horse loose in the middle of it — and organized the Larrow Valley Cooperative Creamery Association. They were tired of hauling butter to Ashlin and taking whatever the merchant allowed for it. Gideon Vose, a heavy, quiet, obstinate man who had once thought of the law and thought better of it, was elected president and held the office twenty-two years, to 1911; he died in 1917. In 1891 the creamery was built at Larrow Green on Larrow Creek — the same building still — and the valley began to be paid cash once a month, which had never happened to it before. Vose wrote the by-laws himself, at his own kitchen table, in a hand the clerks were still complaining about thirty years later.

Article VII is the hinge of everything that follows, and it is worth having entire: *"Every patron shall be paid for the milk he delivers according to the number of pounds of butter fat contained in it, ascertained by test, and not according to the weight of the milk; and the test of the station where he delivers shall govern."* Two halves, and the valley only ever quoted the first. The first half is just: a man is paid for what he actually brings and not for the water naturally in it. The second half — *the test of the station where he delivers shall govern* — makes the test made at a man's own delivery point final. ### Story 5 — The Circular of 1919 and the Ten Years' Silence

**Who.** Selby Vose, manager of the Association from 1913, son of Gideon Vose who wrote Article VII; Ansel and Orra Keddie; Emmet Brant; Bertram Kyle, the clerk who typed it.

**What happened, and when.** In **June 1919** the manager sent a printed circular over his own signature — and no one else's — to the patrons of the Ostrey Hollow station, warning them in temperate language that added water would be looked for and would be dealt with. Kyle typed it, remembered typing it, thought at the time it was a hard thing to send to men bringing milk in every morning of their lives, and typed it anyway. Vose defended it in his annual address of 1926 and said he would write every word of it again tomorrow: "A manager who sees his figures going one way for twenty years and says nothing to the men who make them is not being kind to them; he is being idle at their expense."

- **Recorded station average: 3.61** — the test book's 1922 summary leaf, transcribed identically in three retellings. Teague and Frick both say 3.16 — a transposition; see E1.
- **Milk received, 25 full delivery years 1898–1922: 40,000,000 lb** (1,600,000 lb/yr) — Association ledgers via Loomis, Kyle, Nym, Ivy, Vaught. Teague's and Rundle's 44,000,000 is refuted by Teague's own quoted entry; see E1.

### C1

**(a) Proportion.** The pipettes were blown and marked to deliver 17.6 c.c. and actually delivered a mean of 16.72 c.c.

  16.72 ÷ 17.6 = **0.95 exactly** (check: 17.6 × 0.95 = 16.72).
  Shortfall 17.6 − 16.72 = 0.88 c.c.; 0.88 ÷ 17.6 = 0.05.

**Every test made on that glass read 95% of the truth — low by one part in twenty (5%).** How you get it from the glassware: the neck of the test bottle is ruled to read percent for a 17.6 c.c. charge and no other charge; a short charge liberates proportionally less fat and stands a proportionally shorter column in a neck that knows nothing of the substitution. The reading is therefore low in the exact proportion the charge was short. The error is a *ratio*, not a fixed number of points.
